slide.title: Writing for the Ear
slide.body: AI Voice, Audio and Music · Lesson 2 of 10

scenes.voiceover: In the last lesson, you met the three families of audio AI. Today, we focus on the words you give a voice. A reader controls the speed. They can look back, read a long sentence twice, and see brackets and headings.

scenes.stock_query: person listening to headphones while walking
scenes.voiceover: A listener cannot do any of this. They hear each word once, in order, at the speed of the voice. This is true for a human voice, and even more true for a text-to-speech voice, which reads exactly what you write. So here are five habits that help.

slide.title: Five habits: 1 and 2
slide.body: 1. Short sentences: about 10–20 words; split at 'which', 'although', brackets. 2. One idea at a time: key words at the end of the sentence.

scenes.voiceover: One, short sentences. Aim for about ten to twenty words. If a sentence has which, although or brackets in the middle, split it. Two, one idea at a time. Give each sentence one main point, and put the most important words at the end, where the voice naturally lands.

slide.title: Five habits: 3 and 4
slide.body: 3. Spoken numbers: '2,450 objects' → 'about two and a half thousand objects'; '14/3' → 'the fourteenth of March'. 4. Clear signposts: 'First…' · 'Next…' · 'Now look to your left.'

scenes.voiceover: Three, spoken numbers. Round them when you can, and write them the way you want them said. About two and a half thousand objects is easier to hear than the exact figure. Four, clear signposts. First. Next. Now look to your left. Signposts replace the headings a reader would see.

slide.title: Five habits: 5
slide.body: 5. Pauses and pronunciation: full stops and paragraph breaks = pauses · phonetic spelling, e.g. Tutankhamun (TOOT-ank-AH-moon) · remove 'see Figure 3', links, 'e.g.', '&', '%'

scenes.voiceover: Five, help with pauses and pronunciation. Use full stops and paragraph breaks where you want a pause. For a difficult name, add a phonetic spelling. That is a simple respelling that shows how to say the word. And remove what the ear cannot use, like links, abbreviations and symbols.

slide.title: Map or guide?
slide.body: Left: a folded map showing a whole route, labelled 'Written text'. Right: a guide walking beside a visitor, pointing to the next turn, labelled 'Spoken script'.

scenes.voiceover: Here is a way to picture it. Written text is like a map. The reader sees the whole route at once. A spoken script is like a guide walking beside you. The guide must say each turn at the right moment, one step at a time, because you cannot see the whole route.

scenes.stock_query: museum display case ancient Egyptian stone carving
scenes.voiceover: Let's try it. Nour works for a museum in Cairo, in Egypt. She is preparing an audio guide for one display case. The original label is thirty-five words in one sentence, with a bracket, an abbreviation, a date and two difficult names.

slide.title: The original label
slide.body: "This limestone stela (c. 1350 BCE), discovered in 1912 at Amarna, depicts the royal family beneath the rays of the Aten, a key feature of the religious reforms introduced during the reign of Akhenaten." Highlight in red: the bracket, 'c.', 'BCE', '1912', the two names.

scenes.voiceover: You can see it on screen now. It works on a printed label. But try to hear it, and the listener is lost before the end. So Nour rewrites it for the ear.

slide.title: Rewritten for the ear
slide.body: Short lines, one per sentence, revealed as spoken: 'Look at the flat stone in front of you.' · 'It is called a stela.' · 'It is more than three thousand years old.' · 'It shows a royal family.' · '…That sun is the Aten (AH-ten).' · 'King Akhenaten (ak-en-AH-ten) made the Aten the centre of religious life in Egypt.'

scenes.voiceover: Look at the flat stone in front of you. It is called a stela. It is more than three thousand years old. It shows a royal family. Above them, you can see long lines coming down from a sun. That sun is the Aten. King Akhenaten made the Aten the centre of religious life in Egypt.

slide.title: What changed
slide.body: Before: 35 words, one sentence, 'c. 1350 BCE', bracket. After: short sentences, signpost 'Look at…', 'more than three thousand years old'. Discovery date → printed label.

scenes.voiceover: Notice what changed. Each sentence has one idea. It starts with a signpost, look at. And the old date became more than three thousand years old, which a listener understands at once. The discovery date moved to the printed label.

slide.title: Phonetic spellings as notes
slide.body: Script with pronunciation notes in the margin → arrow → clean text in the TTS box → speaker icon. A small loop: 'Name said wrongly? Add the respelling.'

scenes.voiceover: Nour kept the phonetic spellings as notes and left them out of the text she typed into the text-to-speech tool. She only added them when the tool said a name wrongly.

A common mistake is to paste written text straight into a voice tool. The voice may be good, but the script is not. Rewrite first, then generate. And read it aloud yourself. If you stumble, the listener will stumble too.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Short sentences · one idea · signposts. 2. Numbers, dates, symbols written as spoken; round when you can. 3. Full stops for pauses · phonetic spellings for names

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, listeners hear each word once, so use short sentences, one idea at a time and clear signposts. Second, write numbers, dates and symbols the way you want them said, and round numbers when you can. Third, use full stops for pauses, and phonetic spellings for difficult names.

Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, you will rewrite a written paragraph of about one hundred and fifty words as a spoken script. Then you read it aloud and mark where you need to breathe. It takes about twenty minutes. Keep your script. In the next lesson, Making a Voiceover with Free Text-to-Speech, you will give it a voice.
